children: The U.K. government borrowed more in August than a year earlier, a setback for its plans to reduce its deficit as it prepares to outline a new budget next month.

The Office for National Statistics said Tuesday that government spending exceeded its revenues by 18.3 billion pounds ($24.46 billion), an increase in the budget deficit of 2.9 billion pounds from August 2025.

For the fiscal year to date, borrowing totaled 77.3 billion pounds, a decline of 2.2 billion pounds compared with the same period last year, but 8.1 billion pounds above projections published by the Office for Budget Responsibility in March.
The figures are a blow for the government as it prepares to deliver its next budget on Oct. 28, which will be the first to reflect the policies of Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

While they suggest that the government is on track to reduce its budget deficit for the fiscal year ending in early April 2027, it seems unlikely to make as much progress as the OBR expected without further measures.

The government is bringing in more revenue following earlier tax changes, with receipts up 3.7 billion pounds in August from a year earlier. However, spending has risen much faster, and was up 6.7 billion pounds.

Around the world, government bond yields have risen over recent weeks. That largely reflects an increased likelihood that inflation will stay high for longer than previously anticipated by investors as a result of the U.S.-Iran war and its impact on energy prices.

However, investors are also growing concerned about the rapid rise in debt levels. The U.K. has made some progress toward containing its debts, having in the last fiscal year shrunk  its deficit to its smallest size since the Covid-19 pandemic struck. In August, its debts stood at 93.8% of gross domestic product, down from 95.1% a year earlier.

The OBR expects the budget deficit to fall to 3.6% of gross domestic product this year from 4.3% in the last fiscal year. By contrast, the U.S. deficit has been around 6% of GDP over recent years, and isn't expected to fall significantly below that level.
Higher yields make it more difficult for the government to narrow its budget deficit, since they raise the cost of making interest payments as new bonds are issued to replace maturing securities.

The government could receive a small boost from the Bank of England's review of its program for reducing its holdings of government bonds, which were acquired in the years following the global financial crisis of 2008-09 and then during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Announced last week, the review will be concluded in April 2027, and bond sales will be suspended until then. Until now, the BOE has sold its bonds directly to investors, effectively competing with the government.
